summary:
Cajamarca is a region of Peru and has no trans-specific statute, ordinance or documented incident series in the sources; the binding framework is Peru's national legislation, and none of the sources examined contains Cajamarca-specific content.

Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising. On 2 April 2025 the plenary of Congress approved the fused text of the Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los niños y adolescentes and waived a second vote. Its Article 5.1 prohibits any person from entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than their birth sex, and the same package obliges venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs while banning inclusive wording such as 'women in their diversity'.

The provision traces to the Comisión de Mujer y Familia, which on 20 February 2025 approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante. The text carried narrow exceptions covering custody and situations where entry is required, including accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities. Infobae Peru reports the trigger as a July 2023 complaint over gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chávez international airport.

Practical enforcement would rest on security staff checking the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender, the framing used by activist Gianna Camacho. A consumer-protection body has already applied the underlying logic in private life: SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022 dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against the gym chain SmartFit, which assigned bathroom access on the basis of the sex recorded in the DNI. On television, Willax TV presenter Ana María Salcedo publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru reads Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination under Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors. The institute frames the provision as openly discriminatory against trans and non-binary people and recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

Gender-identity recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive, which shapes what a trans visitor can expect when documents and facilities are checked.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The annual report of the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia recorded 54 assassinations of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases between 2020 and 2023, the homicide victims comprising 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian. Nineteen killings occurred in 2023 alone, 12 of them trans women, and the killers were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides, including 13 of the 19 in 2023. In February 2023 the trans sex worker Rubi Torres Silvano, 31, was kidnapped from central Lima by a 'Los Gallegos' extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots, days after Priscila Aguado Huatuco, 30, was shot; two killers were arrested in March 2023. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising with trans women most affected, and its co-author Gianna Camacho stressed that recorded figures are only a sub-registry. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack; it was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history.

The state has not incorporated sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures, leaving Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.
tangentialFactors:
The bathroom regime reaches beyond state facilities. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's complaint against a gym enforcing DNI-based restroom assignment, and a television presenter used the policy to harass a sitting member of Congress, indicating that the restriction is applied by private businesses and invoked in public commentary as well as by law.

Speech and association are constrained alongside facilities access. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

The national framework runs against regional and international standards. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy, while the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights carried the Azul Rojas Marín case to the Court, producing the region's first torture-by-discrimination judgment.

Comparative positioning is narrow: with Paraguay and Guyana, Peru is one of only three South American countries whose hate-crime law lacks LGBT anti-discrimination coverage, and its recorded hate-crime figures are a sub-registry rather than a count, since sexual orientation and gender identity are absent from crime-registration systems.
localsOnly:
Residents of Cajamarca live under the same national rules as visitors: Article 5.1 of the April 2025 law bars entry to public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than the birth sex, and venues are obliged not to post ambiguous restroom signs.

Gender-identity recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive, so changing the sex marker on the DNI, the document security staff consult at restroom entrances and that businesses such as gyms rely on, is a protracted process for residents as well.

Healthcare access improved on paper in June 2024, when Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, a change directed at trans patients in health settings nationwide.

Because sexual orientation and gender identity are absent from state crime-registration systems, a resident reporting an identity-motivated attack cannot have it recorded or prosecuted as a hate crime, even though 54 TLGBI people were killed between 2020 and 2023.

Residents share the censorship exposure created by the April 2025 law's child-protection articles, including the article 4 ban on media and advertising content and the raised obscenity minimum of four years' imprisonment.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory records Cajamarca-specific enforcement of Article 5.1, local incidents, or statements by the regional authorities; whether the department has issued its own implementing rules is unresolved on the sources reviewed.

The sources do not show how restroom access is policed in practice in Cajamarca, beyond the general expectation reported by Gianna Camacho that security staff would consult the DNI, nor whether any Cajamarca venue has been complained about.

No Cajamarca hate-crime or homicide figures appear in the inventory; the 54 killings and 170 violation cases for 2020-2023 are national totals from the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI and cannot be attributed to this region.

Whether the June 2024 health-guidance change has been applied in Cajamarca's facilities, and whether any local court has ruled on the anti-equality decree struck down in Lima in July 2025, are not sourced.

The inventory does not document the current status of gender-marker changes through Peruvian consulates or migration channels for entering visitors, an unresolved point for entry screening.
